docs.title: How a change to shared code lands
docs.text:
1. Edit the canonical file in the hub.
  2. scripts/revendor_shared.sh copies it into every sibling checkout (--check verifies only; --repo NAME narrows it), re-diffs exactly as CI will, and runs each --selftest against the vendored copy.
  3. Commit the tool-repository copies and the hub edit in one window, then move the hub's v1 tag — never before the copies have landed, or every tool repository's CI goes red at once.

Who owns each shared component (including the files one tool copies from another, and the vocabulary), how a consumer records the revision it adopted, which changes need AMČR's agreement, and the pull request checklist are in the hub's shared_components.md.

The script exits 0 only when CI would pass. A sibling checkout it cannot find is reported as SKIP and still exits 1: parity is unknown for it, not clean.

docs.title: Where the boundaries are
docs.text:
A tool repository never edits a vendored file. A one-byte difference fails para-drift. The formatter is fenced off too: each tool's ruff.toml excludes the vendored files with force-exclude = true, because on one occasion ruff format split test_document_originators.py into two variants across repositories.

The hub never owns tool behaviour. It owns the record's contract, the service contract and the CI; what a tool does is decided in the tool repository.

There is no cross-repository token. A push to a tool repository cannot trigger anything in the hub. The hub re-reads on schedules and on manual dispatch instead.

At run time, the only contract between tools is the record. No tool imports another tool's code. Stages meet in the atrium_document JSON — see The document contract — and in three directories of files.

docs.title: The document contract
docs.text:
The atrium_document record is the one thing that travels through the whole pipeline. This page says what it holds, who may write which part of it, how it is built up stage by stage, and how page-classification and the translator write it.

Normative text lives in the hub

docs/document_schema.md is the specification. This page explains it, with page-classification and the translator as the worked cases.

docs.title: The object
docs.text:
One JSON file per document, named <doc_id>.document.json, schema version 1.0 (frozen as doc-schema-v1). The module that writes it, atrium_document.py, is vendored byte-identically into every tool, so every tool writes the record the same way; what differs is which calls each tool makes.

Part What it holds schema_version, record_type, doc_id identity — record_type is atrium-document, or atrium-document-merged for a merge of parallel branches source the original input: its identifier, checksum and how it was acquired (source.origin) provenance contributors[] — every run that wrote to it — and a computed licence label (see below), not a licence assembled one stamp per block: who wrote it last, in which run page_categories, pages, content, lines, tables, quality_summary, entities, translations, enrichment, keywords, forms the tool blocks — one authorised writer each, see Repository map derived_from references to persistent outputs a stage produced regenerable recipes for disposable outputs, never their paths

Five keys are required: schema_version, record_type, doc_id, provenance, assembled. Six are reserved — no tool can set_block() them: those five and source. The schema adds one consistency rule worth knowing: any block named in assembled.blocks must exist at the top level, so a record cannot claim a contribution it does not contain.

docs.title: The stamp, and the contributor list
docs.text:
Every write stamps the block it touched:

"assembled": { "blocks": { "<block>": {
  "program": "…", "run_id": "…", "paradata_ref": "…", "updated_at": "…" } } }

and every run that wrote anything appends itself once:

"provenance": { "contributors": [ {
  "program": "…", "run_id": "…", "paradata_ref": "…",
  "blocks": "page_categories,pages", "at": "…" } ] }

blocks is a comma-separated string, not a list. The stamp names only the most recent writer of a block, so for a block several programs write fields of — pages[], entities[] — contributors[] is the only complete account.

docs.title: The life of a record
docs.text:
1. Load. A stage opens the record it was given with --document-json — the baseline — or starts a new one. A baseline written by a newer major schema version is refused; an older one is migrated.
  2. Write. The stage writes only the blocks it owns: set_block() replaces a whole block, merge_block() updates chosen fields inside a keyed list such as pages[]. Everything else in the baseline is carried through untouched.
  3. Stamp. Each written block gets its assembled.blocks stamp, the run is added to provenance.contributors[], and the run's list of components with their licences is added to the record's.
  4. Validate. The finished record is checked against atrium_document.schema.json; a stage never emits a record that fails its own schema.
  5. Write out. The file is written atomically — to a temporary name, then renamed — so a reader never sees half a record.

The next stage repeats the cycle with this file as its baseline.

docs.title: The six rules, per tool
docs.text:
The rules are the hub's; the right-hand columns show how each tool applies them.

Rule page-classification translator 1 · Baseline in, record out Opt-in. No record is written unless --document-json-out or --document-json-out-dir is set (or their [DOCUMENT] config keys). Writes the file itself, atomically, rather than through finalize() Always writes one, by default as <doc_id>.document.json next to its output, baseline or not 2 · Own block only set_block("page_categories", …) merged with the baseline's categories — page keys from an earlier run survive — plus a keyed merge_block("pages", …) restricted to category and category_confidence set_block("translations", …) and add_derived_from("translated_xml", …) 3 · No baseline → own part only derives doc_id from the filename: a trailing -N or _N is the page, the rest is the document (scan_0007.png → document scan, page "7"); no suffix means page 1, with a warning inherits doc_id from the baseline — its input is a page, <doc>-1.alto.xml, so deriving it would re-key the document — and derives it only when there is no baseline 4 · Per-block provenance stamps page_categories, pages, and derived_from when it records a result table stamps translations and derived_from 5 · Licences accrete contributes its paradata licence block; see below contributes its paradata licence block; see below 6 · Unknown blocks preserved ✓ through the shared module ✓ through the shared module

docs.title: What the record says about licences
docs.text:
Each run adds to the record the list of components it used (models, data, vocabularies, services), each with its own licence or terms of use, as its paradata recorded them. From all the lists so far, the shared para_licenses module computes one label, the most restrictive licence among them, and writes it as provenance.license. provenance.license_detail keeps the lists the label came from.

The label is not the licence of the record or of anything in it. A component's licence does not become the licence of what the component produced, and the rights in a record depend first on the source document. Licences and paradata explains this in plain words, and what is proposed instead (#6). Until that changes, read provenance.license as "the most restrictive licence among the components used".

For the two tools of this page: a page-classification inference run lists vit_models (MIT) as its only always-used component (the training dataset counts only for --train, which writes no record). A translator run with the default backend and vocabulary lists CUBBITT, UDPipe, AMČR and TEATER; with the UDPipe models under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, the label reads CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. A record with no component list at all gets the fallback label CC BY-NC 4.0, and provenance.license_note says so.

docs.title: What the references point at
docs.text:
Only source and derived_from may reference files, and only persistent ones. What the two tools put there:

Field page-classification translator derived_from classification — the run's result table, one CSV for the whole run (or one per day when --chunk is on); absent for a single-file run translated_xml — the translated file's name, such as CTX000000003-1_en.alto.xml paradata_ref the run's paradata file; empty for records written by the service, which keeps no paradata file the run's paradata file under <output>/paradata/; in the service, the per-request paradata, not kept

docs.title: Over HTTP
docs.text:
Both services can accrete onto a record uploaded with the request — as a multipart part named document_json — and they return it differently:

page-classification translator Returns the record inside its JSON response, as document_json as the second part of a multipart/mixed response, after the translated XML Without a baseline only if document_json_out=true is sent — it can originate a record only with a baseline — over HTTP it extends records rather than starting them Its own output fails the schema (baseline valid) refused with a 500 refused with a 500

After page-classification (-f CTX000000003-1.png --document-json-out 1_pc.json, no baseline):

  },

Then the translator takes that record as --document-json and writes:

{
  "derived_from": {"translated_xml": "CTX000000003-1_en.alto.xml"},
  "translations": {"source_lang": "cs", "target_lang": "en", "backend": "lindat", "output_mode": "replace"},
  "assembled":  {"blocks": {"translations": {"program": "translator", "…": "…"},
                            "derived_from": {"program": "translator", "…": "…"}},
                 "had_baseline": true},
  "provenance": {"license": "…", "license_detail": "…",
                 "contributors": [ "…page-classification…",
                                   {"program": "translator", "blocks": "translations,derived_from", "…": "…"} ]}
}

page_categories and pages pass through untouched (rule 2); the translator adds its blocks, its stamps and itself to contributors[], and its component list joins page-classification's in the label provenance.license (rule 5). The values in page_categories are the eleven labels.

docs.title: How paradata accumulates
docs.text:
Every run writes its own paradata file: a log of that run. It says which program and version ran, when, with which settings, which components it used and with which licences, how long it took, and counts of what it processed. The record does not copy it; it points to it. Each run that writes to the record adds itself to provenance.contributors[] with a paradata_ref, and each block it wrote is stamped with the same reference. So a record's paradata accumulates as a list of pointers, one per run, and following them gives the whole history of the record.

The file is written by the shared atrium_paradata.py, format version 2.0: a flat JSON object with tool_version, run_id, start_time, license_detail, the configuration and statistics at the top level. Every field is in docs/paradata_schema.md.

Both formats follow the same rule for changes: an additive change keeps the version; a breaking one raises the major version and ships a _migrate_X_to_Y() function. A reader refuses a file with a newer major version than it knows, and migrates an older one.

docs.title: Licences and paradata
docs.text: This page explains, without code, what the ATRIUM tools record about the software, models and data they use, what the one licence they compute means and does not mean, and what replaces it.

docs.title: What a run records
docs.text:
Every run of an ATRIUM tool writes a short log, its paradata. It says which program and version ran, when, with which settings, and what it produced. It also lists the components the run used: the models, datasets, vocabularies and web services. Each component is listed with its own licence, or, for a web service, the terms of use it is offered under.

The document record that travels through the pipeline points to the paradata of every run that wrote to it. So for any record you can find out which tools touched it and what each of them used.

docs.title: The licence the tools compute, and what it is not
docs.text:
From that list of components, the shared module para_licenses.py also computes one label: the most restrictive of the component licences, on a scale from public domain to CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. It was added as a warning. If a run used a model published for non-commercial use, the label says so at a glance. The record carries the label as provenance.license, and an RO-Crate export states it as the licence of the crate.

The label is not the licence of the output, and should not be read as one:

  • A licence covers what it is attached to: a program, a model or a dataset. Using a tool does not put what it produces under the tool's licence.
  • Web services have terms of use, not a licence for their output. LINDAT, for example, licenses its software and models and offers its services under Terms of Use.
  • "The strictest wins" says nothing about compatibility. Some licences cannot be combined at all. Picking the strictest one does not show that the others are respected.
  • Using a component is not, by itself, making a derived work of it. For example, tagging a line with one term from a vocabulary. Whether an output is a derived work is a legal question, and the label cannot answer it.
  • The rights in an output depend first on the source document. No tool knows those rights.

The tools' pages now list each component with its licence or terms. They do not say that a result "is" under any licence.

docs.title: What changes
docs.text:
The proposal on #6 keeps what is useful and drops the label:

  1. Keep the list of components, each with its own licence or terms and where that was read, and make it more precise.
  2. Record which processing policy allowed the run. The deployment's operator (AMČR, for the pilot) writes the policy: for example, whether texts may be sent to an external service. Each document also carries its own permission, and a document without one is not sent to an external service.
  3. State the rights in an output only when someone entitled to do so asserts them. Without that, the rights are unknown, and the record says nothing.

AMČR agreed to this on 22 October 2026: AMČR states the rights of the outputs it publishes, and no tool makes an automatic or default licence assertion. The shared modules change next, first where records and crates still state the computed label. Until then, read provenance.license as "the most restrictive licence among the components used", nothing more.

Where a repository has no tool section in Docs here, its own README.md is the reference; its workflow page gives the stable core of what it does, and its landing page links to both.

Of the two documented tools, both are MIT-licensed code. page-classification runs its models locally — on CPU, or faster on a CUDA GPU; the translator calls remote LINDAT services by default and needs no GPU unless a self-hosted CTranslate2 model is chosen.

The order is accretion order, not a chain of file handoffs

The rows are in the order a document record travels — page-classification writes first, keyword-extract last. That is not the order files move in. Only three real file handoffs exist (PAGE_ALTO/, DOC_LINE_CATEG/, TEITOK/), the translator's output is an end product rather than an input to a later stage, and page_categories informs a routing decision rather than feeding a program. Pipelines draws both layers.

docs.title: Who may write which block
docs.text:
Every block of the atrium_document record has exactly one authorised writer, declared once in the hub-canonical BLOCK_OWNERS and vendored byte-identically into every tool:

Block Authorised writer page_categories page-classification pages, content, lines, tables ocr-postprocess or digital-convert — one of the two, fixed per document translations translator entities nlp-enrich enrichment, forms keyword-extract (llm-enrich in records written before 1 October 2026) keywords keyword-extract — the statistical kind, beside enrichment, never in one list quality_summary ocr-postprocess — on every origin, as the quality model's owner

Shared blocks are split by field rather than by block: page-classification may write only category and category_confidence inside pages[], and the translator only translation_en inside entities[] — a field the schema reserves for it; entities themselves are created later, by nlp-enrich.

docs.title: The positional plane has two possible originators
docs.text:
pages, content, lines and tables — the positional plane — can be written by either of two programs, and which one is decided per document by source.origin, through ORIGIN_ORIGINATORS:

source.origin starts with Originator digital-born · docx · pdf digital-convert ABBYY-ALTO · ocr: · vlm: ocr-postprocess

Matching is a case-insensitive prefix match, first match wins. An origin that matches nothing does not raise — the check simply abstains, so a new origin string can land before the table learns about it.

ocr-postprocess records a truthful origin per input format: ABBYY-ALTO for ALTO, ocr:<format> for the other OCR formats (PAGE XML, hOCR, ABBYY FineReader XML, DjVuXML, Tesseract TSV, a PDF's OCR layer), ocr:generic for text whose making the file does not record, and digital-born-<kind> for the born-digital documents it reads. For a born-digital document it writes source only and leaves the plane to digital-convert — which reads PDF, DOCX, ODT, ODS, XLSX, RTF, DOC and XLS (since its v1.1.0-beta), so a born-digital slide deck, ODP, EPUB, HTML page or e-mail gets no positional plane yet. The per-format list is in ocr-postprocess's input formats reference.

Program ids and repositories

The program id in a record names the role, not the repository, and a repository move does not rewrite it. Two ids have a successor since 1 October 2026: alto-postprocess continues as ocr-postprocess, and llm-enrich was split — its keyword stage continues as keyword-extract, while its born-digital converter keeps the role id digital-convert and has its own repository. The hub's PROGRAM_SUCCESSORS map adds each successor beside its predecessor as an allowed writer: a record written before the move keeps its stamps, loads, merges and passes the origin check, and nothing already written is re-attributed. One page per tool, telling its workflow from beginning to end: what it is for, each step with the formats that go in and come out, what the user ends up with, what licence that result carries, and where the same workflow is published on other platforms.

Pipelines shows how the tools connect to each other. These pages take one tool at a time and describe it the way a person using only that tool meets it.

docs.text:
Tool Depth What the workflow does SSH Open Marketplace page-classification full sorts scanned archive pages into eleven categories that decide how each page is processed next tool RER7Fw ocr-postprocess stable core turns OCR output into per-page text and a table of text lines labelled by language and OCR quality tool YParYU translator full translates the text inside XML documents and writes it back without changing their structure tool CizIUW · workflow 13eHAZ nlp-enrich stable core adds lemmas, part-of-speech tags, syntax and named entities to text lines, and writes TEITOK XML tool EMhu3X keyword-extract stable core finds statistical keywords, and maps text onto the AMČR and TEATER vocabularies with a language model tool j9fqxo digital-convert stable core reads born-digital PDF, DOCX, ODT, ODS, XLSX and RTF files (DOC and XLS through LibreOffice) into the document record without OCR, and flags pages that need OCR tool jGxgQI

docs.title: What every narrative contains
docs.text:
The sections are fixed, so that the same text can be pasted into a workflow record without being rewritten, and so that a reader who has read one narrative can find their way in the next.

  1. Purpose — what the workflow is for, in one paragraph.
  2. At a glance — inputs and outputs with their formats, the ways the tool runs, the hardware it needs, what it reaches over the network, the licence of the code and the rule for the licence of the output.
  3. Steps — numbered. Each step says what happens, what goes in and what comes out (with formats), and the research activity it performs, named with the TaDiRAH terms the SSH Open Marketplace uses.
  4. What you get — the outputs, and how to read them.
  5. Limits — what follows from how the tool works. Nothing here describes the state of work in progress.
  6. Provenance and licence — the paradata log every run writes, the block the tool owns in the document record, and how the licence of a run is computed.
  7. Where it sits — the cross-tool workflows on Pipelines the tool takes part in, and its step in the AMČR chain.
  8. On other platforms — its SSH Open Marketplace records and a Galaxy sheet: the Galaxy datatypes of its inputs and outputs, the container, compute and network needs, test data, and the closest tools already available in Galaxy.
  9. Sources — what the page was written from, and at which release.

They give the purpose, the order of the steps, the formats, the licence floor and the records, and leave out thresholds, default models and options that are not part of a release. docs.title: Reading born-digital documents into the document record, without OCR
docs.text:
The digital-convert workflow. Tool: atrium-digital-convert. The tool was part of llm-enrich until 1 October 2026; it continues in a new repository under its own name, and the keyword extraction that llm-enrich also did moved to keyword-extract.

Scope

This page gives the stable core of the workflow: its purpose, its steps, the formats it reads and writes, and the licence floor of its output. The converter's engines and options, the rules that route a page, and the service's limits and settings with their defaults are documented with the code — in the tool's README, whose documentation map leads to its usage, configuration and how-it-works pages, and its service README — because they change as the rules are calibrated on AMČR documents.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A PDF, a word-processor file or a spreadsheet that was never printed and scanned already carries its text; running OCR on it would only add errors. This workflow reads such a file directly and writes the ATRIUM document record from what it finds: the pages, the lines (with their boxes, in a PDF), the blocks they belong to, the headings, running headers and footers, footnotes and tables. It also checks the text layer of every page. A page whose layer is missing, does not decode to readable text or comes from an earlier OCR run is flagged needs_ocr, so that the orchestration can send those pages to OCR; on request the tool also assesses every page and says where it should go next. A PDF whose text layer is mostly the result of an earlier OCR run is refused, because it belongs to the OCR route and ocr-postprocess.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: In PDF, DOCX, ODT, ODS, XLSX and RTF files, and DOC/XLS through LibreOffice, recognised by their content, not their extension; optionally the AMČR seed record, whose source.sha512 must match the file Out the ATRIUM document record (JSON); on request the same record as annotated Markdown; a per-page assessment (JSON), from /describe or, since v1.3.0-beta, the command line's --describe; the run's paradata (JSON) Runs as an HTTP service, api-digital (image -api: POST /reformat, and POST /describe for a per-page assessment), and a command-line tool (api_util/digital_to_json.py, image -digital), under these names since v1.1.0-beta Compute CPU, no GPU; memory follows the text a document holds, not its file size; the optional layout-model engine for complex PDFs is a local, opt-in build Network none for /reformat and a plain command-line run; /describe (--describe) calls page-classification and ocr-postprocess when their URLs are set; the optional layout-model engine fetches its models at build time Code licence MIT Component licences the default engine uses permissively licensed libraries; the optional layout-model engine adds model weights under Apache-2.0 and CDLA-Permissive-2.0; LibreOffice, which converts DOC and XLS, is listed. The rights in the text are the source document's: Licences and paradata Record SSH Open Marketplace tool jGxgQI

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: # Step What happens In → out Activity 1 Read the file When an AMČR seed is sent, its source.sha512 is checked against the file's bytes first, and a mismatch is refused. The type is recognised from the content. A light engine reads the PDF or DOCX structure directly; for complex PDFs a layout-model engine can be selected instead. ODT, ODS, XLSX and RTF go through the reader shared with ocr-postprocess; DOC and XLS are first converted to DOCX and XLSX by headless LibreOffice. PDF, DOCX, ODT, ODS, XLSX, RTF, DOC, XLS → IR Converting 2 Check the text layer Every page's text layer is tested and its verdict recorded as text_layer (digital, garbled, ocr, none, blank); a line that does not decode is marked Garbage. A page without a usable layer is marked needs_ocr with its reason; a PDF whose layer is mostly an earlier OCR run is refused with a registered reason and no record. IR → IR — 3 Build the record Pages, lines with their block ids (and exact boxes in a PDF; the other formats have none), line styles (heading level, bold and italic, running header or footer, footnote), tables and the source's identity are written as the blocks the tool owns. In a PDF a heading is a line set larger than the body text, or a bold line at the body size that reads as a title, unless bold body-size text is more than BOLD_HEADING_MAX_SHARE of the body text. The record is written only if it keeps to the tool's own fields and passes the schema. IR → JSON Converting 4 Assess the pages, when asked for /describe, or the command line's --describe, says for every page whether its text can be used as it is, what kind of page it is (page-classification), whether its text reads (ocr-postprocess), and its route: nlp (use the text), ocr or htr (re-acquire it, for handwriting with HTR) or none (nothing to read). The two stages are called only when their URLs are set, and may add their own fields to the record; without them the tool answers from the converter alone. A stage that is down is reported, never a failed request. JSON → JSON — 5 Render, when asked for The record is turned into annotated Markdown, page by page in reading order, with the layout carried in HTML comments: the one form in which a document is given to a language model, as in keyword-extract's whole-document runs. JSON → Markdown —

docs.title: Provenance and licence
docs.text:
Every /reformat and /describe call returns the run's paradata: an RO-Crate CreateAction that names the file it read, with its digest, the seed when one was sent, and the record blocks it wrote; /describe adds each stage's own paradata. On the command line, --paradata-dir writes a paradata log (JSON). The paradata lists the components that ran, each with its licence, as declared in the tool's para_config.txt: with the default engine, permissively licensed libraries only, so the computed label is MIT, and the layout-model engine keeps it there. LibreOffice is declared but left out of the label: it changes the container of a text it does not author, and the conversion is reported beside the record instead. The label is not the licence of the output: the source document's own rights apply to its text (Licences and paradata).

In the document record the tool is one of the two originators of the positional layer — pages, content, lines and tables — for a born-digital document, as ocr-postprocess is for a scanned one; the document's source.origin decides which of the two writes. The one exception is a page flagged needs_ocr, whose lines ocr-postprocess may replace with the OCR lines. Every page row also carries the converter's text_layer. In /describe, page-classification and ocr-postprocess may add their own fields (page categories, line and page quality); the tool keeps their write only when its own part of the record comes back unchanged. The program id in the record is digital-convert, as before the move.

docs.title: Where it sits
docs.text:
• First stage of the born-digital route — Pipelines → W2. Scans and images go through OCR and ocr-postprocess instead; the route step of the AMČR pipeline chooses by the file type AMČR detected. That route calls /reformat, which calls no other service: in the AMČR deployment Temporal chains the stages.
  • The OCR hand-off — Pipelines → W3. Pages flagged needs_ocr go to the ATR service. /describe refines that list in summary.reacquire_pages: it leaves out drawings and photographs, sends handwriting to HTR, and adds decoding pages whose prose the quality model rejects. A page that loses letters to unmapped glyphs is flagged in the record itself since v1.2.2-beta (garbled), and goes to OCR whatever its page type. ocr-postprocess then merges the ATR ALTO of each flagged page back into the same record, page by page; the born-digital pages stay as the converter wrote them.
  • What follows it. The record goes on to nlp-enrich and keyword-extract, which reads the converter's lines like any other record's.
  • Born-digital extraction step of the AMČR text workflow 0xSpVP (step 6, beside GROBID).
  • The service image is one of the containerised services — Pipelines → W4.

docs.title: Keywords from archival text: statistical, and from the controlled vocabularies
docs.text:
The keyword-extract workflow. Tool: atrium-keyword-extract. It takes over both kinds of keywords that used to be made in two places: the statistical keywords of nlp-enrich and the vocabulary-controlled keywords of llm-enrich. nlp-enrich keeps only the LINDAT calls.

Scope

This page gives the stable core of the workflow: its purpose, its steps, the formats it reads and writes, and the licence floor of its output. The methods' options, the models and the prompts are documented with the code — in the tool's README, whose documentation map leads to its usage, how-it-works and reference pages, and its service README — because they change as methods are compared and chosen. Both kinds now live in the tool: the statistical kind since its first release, the controlled kind since v1.1.0-beta. No controlled category has been checked against a reviewed answer yet, so treat the categories as research output.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Finding an archival document by what it is about needs its keywords, and two kinds answer different questions. Statistical keywords are the phrases that characterise a document or a page against the rest of its text; they need no vocabulary and say how they were found. Controlled keywords are given per line: a language model picks the term of the AMČR keyword lists or the TEATER thesaurus that describes the line, and can only pick a term that exists in the vocabulary. With the term come the records behind it, the Czech keywords found in the line with their English translations, and the page and line it came from. The two kinds are kept apart in the output, and every statistical keyword says which method produced it.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: In the ATRIUM document record, after nlp-enrich; or plain text. Since v1.5.0-beta the statistical kind also reads files, on the command line (keywords.py) and as POST /extract_keywords's file alike: nlp-enrich's CoNLL-U or TEITOK, a line table (CSV) or a .txt. The controlled kind's batch clients read line tables (CSV), TEITOK or records Out statistical keywords with their method, score and rank, per document and per page; controlled keywords per line (JSON); the run's paradata (JSON). With a record sent: the record with its keywords block (statistical kind) and its enrichment block (controlled kind), side by side. The batch CLI writes CSV tables and, on request, each page's keywords (--per-page) and the record's keywords block (--document-json-out-dir), as the service does Runs as an HTTP service image (POST /extract_keywords, /extract_keywords_text), the production image; a command-line tool for the statistical kind (keywords.py) and its image; batch clients for the controlled kind; a research run on GPUs (llm_run.py) and its image Compute CPU for YAKE and the legacy method; a GPU is used by KeyBERT when there is one; the service's controlled kind calls a language-model service and carries no weights; the research run loads a model's weights onto GPUs Network the Hugging Face Hub for the KeyBERT model, on first use (the service fetches it at startup); for the controlled kind, the language-model service (OpenRouter, or a local Ollama). Only the vocabulary build reaches the AMČR and TEATER sources Code licence MIT Component licences KeyBERT (MIT) with its sentence-transformers model (Apache-2.0), YAKE (AGPL-3.0) when chosen, the AMČR and TEATER vocabularies (CC0), and for the controlled kind the language model's own terms; each run lists the ones it used. These do not by themselves set the rights in the output: Licences and paradata Record SSH Open Marketplace tool j9fqxo

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
# Step What happens In → out Activity 1 Select the text The lines of the record are gathered per document and per page. Lines categorised Trash, Garbage, Inverted (a born-digital text layer that does not decode) or Empty are left out. Methods that need linguistic annotation use the lemmas and part-of-speech tags that nlp-enrich wrote. JSON → text — 2 Statistical keywords KeyBERT (the default) ranks candidate phrases by their similarity to the document's embedding; YAKE ranks them without a model; the legacy method counts nouns, proper nouns and adjectives by lemma. Scores differ in meaning per method. text → keywords Keyword extraction 3 Build the vocabulary The AMČR keyword lists and the TEATER thesaurus are harvested and nested into one term list, each term pointing back to the records it came from. This is done once, not per run: each release carries the built vocabulary as a CC0 asset, atrium-vocabulary-<version>.zip, with its .sha256. → JSON, CSV, SKOS Collecting 4 Controlled keywords A language model reads each line among its neighbours on the page and answers with the term that describes it (with the AMČR and TEATER records behind it), the Czech keywords found in it with their English translations, and a confidence. Its answer must fit a schema whose allowed categories are the vocabulary's terms. text → JSON Enriching, Content Analysis 5 Record the result Statistical keywords go into the record's keywords block, each with its method, score and rank; controlled keywords into its enrichment block, one item per line with its page. Entities that are vocabulary terms are linked to AMČR and AAT identifiers. The paradata names the method, the model and the vocabulary sources. → JSON —

Step 2 is the statistical kind and step 4 the controlled one; step 3 is done when the vocabulary is built, and a run reads its result. The request chooses which kind runs (kind=statistical, controlled or both, the default), and each kind can fail or be skipped on its own and says so. The service and the batch clients reach the model through OpenRouter or a local Ollama; the research run llm_run.py loads it onto its own GPUs.

Two limits follow from how the controlled kind works (the service README's Known limits). The schema keeps a category inside the vocabulary, not on topic: a model can be forced onto an unrelated term that shares the start of the word it began. And confidence_score is not calibrated: most lines get one of two values, so do not rank or filter on it.

docs.title: Provenance and licence
docs.text:
Every run records its paradata, which lists the components that ran, each with its licence, as declared in the tool's para_config.txt. The service returns the paradata in its response, as a Process Run Crate CreateAction; the command-line and batch runs write it as a log (JSON), and the controlled ones name the vocabulary build they used. The statistical methods differ: the legacy method uses only the standard library, KeyBERT is MIT and loads a sentence-transformers model (Apache-2.0), and YAKE is AGPL-3.0; a run that selects YAKE lists it. The vocabularies are CC0. The language model is not in that list: its own licence or its provider's terms apply to the controlled kind, and every controlled run records the model's id. The paradata's computed label, the most restrictive of the licences listed, is not the licence of the output: Licences and paradata.

In the document record the tool is the successor of llm-enrich as a writer: the contract lets it write the enrichment and forms blocks and entities[].pid, and, since v1.2.0-beta, the keywords block (atrium-project#73). It writes keywords when the statistical kind ran — the keywords of the document and of each page, every one with its method, score and rank — and enrichment with entities[].pid when the controlled kind contributed; it writes no forms. The two kinds stay in their own blocks and never share a list, and a re-run replaces each block whole. Records already written keep the program id llm-enrich; the contract accepts both names for the one writer.

docs.title: Linguistic annotation and named entities, kept on the page
docs.text:
The nlp-enrich workflow. Tool: atrium-nlp-enrich.

Scope

This page gives the stable core of the workflow: its purpose, its steps, the formats it reads and writes, and the licence floor of its output. The details of the TEITOK output, and the named-entity model in use are documented with the code — in the tool's README and schemas/teitok/README.md — because they change as the format and the models are refined. Keywords are no longer made here: they moved to keyword-extract on 1 October 2026 (release v1.0.0-beta).

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Searching and linking archival documents needs more than their raw text: the base form of each word, its part of speech, the structure of the sentence, and the people, places and organisations it names. This workflow sends the text lines of each document to LINDAT's UDPipe 2 and NameTag 3 services, merges their answers, and writes the result as tables, as CoNLL-U and as TEITOK XML — a TEI-based format that keeps every word tied to its place on the page image when a page layout is supplied: the OCR's ALTO files, a TEITOK file converted by flexiconv, or the record of a born-digital PDF.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: In tables of text lines (CSV or XLSX with a text column) from ocr-postprocess, or plain text (.txt, a form feed starting a page), on the command line and over HTTP alike; or the lines of an ATRIUM document record; optionally, for word positions, the original ALTO files or a TEITOK file converted by flexiconv, and the page images; optionally the ATRIUM document record (JSON) to add to — the record digital-convert writes for a born-digital PDF is a layout too Out CoNLL-U per document; named entities per page (TSV); tokens, lemmas and entities per document (CSV); an entity summary for the collection (CSV); TEITOK XML; a paradata log (JSON); optionally the ATRIUM document record (JSON); over HTTP, a JSON envelope or a ZIP of these files Runs as a command-line pipeline (four stage scripts, or run_pipeline.py); a batch container image; an HTTP service image (/enrich, /enrich_text, /jobs, /rescale, /project_record); an Agent Skill Compute CPU; the annotation itself runs on LINDAT's servers Network the LINDAT UDPipe 2 and NameTag 3 services, or self-hosted ones set by UDPIPE_URL and NAMETAG_URL Code licence MIT Component licences the UDPipe 2 and NameTag 3 models (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), through the LINDAT services and their terms of use, on every run. These do not by themselves set the rights in the output: Licences and paradata Record SSH Open Marketplace tool EMhu3X

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
# Step What happens In → out Activity 1 Collect the text The lines of each document are put in page and line order into one text per document; on request (--skip-untrustworthy-lines, SKIP_UNTRUSTWORTHY_LINES) the lines ocr-postprocess marked Trash, Garbage or Inverted are left out. A rows file keeps the page and line of every line, and a manifest lists the documents. CSV, XLSX, TXT → TXT, TSV — 2 Morphology and syntax UDPipe 2 tokenises the text and adds lemmas, part-of-speech tags, morphological features and dependency syntax. A long text is sent in pieces cut at line ends, and the answers are joined again. TXT → CoNLL-U Lemmatizing, Tagging 3 Named entities NameTag 3 finds names of people, places, organisations and other entities in the annotated text, and writes them page by page; the pages come from the rows file. CoNLL-U → TSV Named Entity Recognition 4 Merge and write Tokens, lemmas and entities are joined per document into tables, into CoNLL-U with the entities added, and into TEITOK XML. With a layout, each word in TEITOK carries its box on the page; without one, TEITOK keeps the pages and lines of the table. Every TEITOK file is checked against the format before the stage ends. CoNLL-U, TSV (+ ALTO, TEITOK, JSON) → CSV, CoNLL-U, TEITOK XML (+ JSON) —

The layout of a document comes from its ALTO file; else from a TEITOK file that flexiconv converted; else from its born-digital record. The record digital-convert writes for a PDF (POST /reformat) has the size of each page and a box for each line. Word boxes are shared out from the line boxes, so they are approximate. The boxes are in PDF points: the command line scales them to the page images (INPUT_PAGES_DIR) or to a resolution (IMAGE_DPI), and the service returns them in points. A DOCX record has no boxes.

An optional stage converts documents that are not ALTO — PDF, office files, PAGE XML, hOCR — into TEITOK; with FLEXICONV_ANNOTATE (or run_pipeline.py --with-flexiconv) they are then annotated like a table (Pipelines → W11). The converter runs from the command line only; the service takes its output as an upload. The tool's projection of the finished record into the TEITOK header (/project_record, opt-in) reads the page categories and the keywords that keyword-extract wrote, so it runs after that step.

Rescaling. POST /rescale (or fix_teitok_bboxes.py on the command line) rewrites the boxes of a finished TEITOK file for page images of another size, page by page. For the points of a born-digital record, give scale = the images' DPI / 72.

When a run stops, the runner's exit code says why, and the service answers with the matching HTTP status. LINDAT not answering after its retries is exit 6 (502 upstream_unavailable); every attempt timing out is exit 7 (504); a TEITOK file that fails its check is exit 5 (500). Before the first stage the runner checks that the stages' python3 can import what they need; if it cannot, it stops with exit 3 (500) and says how to fix it. The usage guide's exit codes list them all.

docs.title: Provenance and licence
docs.text:
The stages write paradata logs, and a whole-pipeline run merges them into one run summary. Over HTTP the run's provenance comes back with the answer, as a Process Run Crate action (paradata). The paradata lists the components a run used, each with its licence, as declared in the tool's para_config.txt. Every core run uses the UDPipe 2 and NameTag 3 models (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) through the LINDAT services, under LINDAT's terms of use; the optional stage declares its own component (the format converter, GPL-3.0). The paradata's computed label is therefore CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for every core run. It is not the licence of the annotations: how the models' licence and the services' terms bear on the output is an open question (#78, #6); see Licences and paradata.

In the document record the tool owns the entities block. Each entity points at its <name> in the TEITOK file (teitok_ref), and each page with a surface at its <surface> (pages[].teitok_surface). When the record cannot be updated, the runner says so ([document-json] NOT WRITTEN) and the service returns null in its place; the other outputs are complete, and the record sent is unchanged.

docs.title: Turning OCR output into clean, classified text lines
docs.text:
The ocr-postprocess workflow. Tool: atrium-ocr-postprocess. The tool was named alto-postprocess until 1 October 2026; it continues in a new repository under the new name, with its code, its pipeline and its categories unchanged.

Scope

This page gives the stable core of the workflow: its purpose, its steps, the formats it reads and writes, and the licence floor of its output. The rules that decide a line's category, their thresholds and the options of each step are documented with the code — in the tool's README and docs/categorization_logic.md — because they change as the rules are calibrated.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: OCR output mixes readable text with lines that were misread, lines that are not text at all, and empty lines. This workflow splits OCR output into pages, extracts the text of each page in reading order, and labels every text line by its language and by how well it was recognised, so that later stages can work on the readable text and send the rest back for another attempt. ALTO is its main input; the other OCR formats, and text-bearing files such as PDF or DOCX, are labelled the same way. It also scores the lines of a born-digital record, so that scanned and born-digital documents get one quality answer. It is the point where the ATRIUM pipeline fans out: the per-page ALTO feeds the translator, the line tables feed the NLP enrichment, and the record feeds keyword extraction.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: In ALTO XML (v2–v4) from OCR; the other OCR formats — PAGE XML, hOCR, ABBYY FineReader XML, DjVuXML, Tesseract TSV, OCR JSON; PDF, office, e-mail and plain-text files, as listed in the tool's input-format reference; for scoring alone, an existing ATRIUM document record (JSON) Out per-page ALTO or JSON, and plain text; page statistics (CSV); per-document tables of text lines with their language, quality score and category (CSV); per-page category counts (CSV); for the other formats, a report of what was read (CSV); a paradata log (JSON); optionally the ATRIUM document record (JSON) Runs as a command-line pipeline (run_pipeline.py, or one script per step), and score_record.py to score the lines of existing records; a container image; an HTTP service image (POST /process, which also merges an OCR'd page into a born-digital record, and POST /score_record to score the lines of an existing record); an Agent Skill Compute the line classification step and the default, layout-aware text extraction are built for a GPU; the service also runs on a CPU and uses a GPU when it finds one; the published images are CPU builds, and a GPU image is built locally from the same Dockerfile Network the Hugging Face Hub for its models on first use; the images already hold the language-identification model Code licence MIT; the vendored alto-tools are Apache-2.0 Component licences the language-identification model (CC BY-NC 4.0) on every run; the layout-aware reading-order model (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) when it orders ALTO lines, as it does by default (see below). These do not by themselves set the rights in the output: Licences and paradata Record SSH Open Marketplace tool YParYU

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
# Step What happens In → out Activity 1 Split into pages ALTO and OCR JSON documents are split into one file per page, named after the document and the page number. Any other file is recognised by its content and read into pages of lines, with a report of what was read and what was refused. ALTO, JSON, other formats → ALTO, JSON, TXT — 2 Build page statistics For every page: its text lines, illustrations, graphics and words, in one table per collection. ALTO, JSON, TXT → CSV — 3 Extract the text The text of each page is extracted by one of five methods: in reading order by a layout-aware model (LayoutReader, the default for ALTO), in ALTO's own order (alto-tools; the service's reading_order=alto), from the page image by a vision-language model (GLM), from the text keys of OCR JSON (json-keys), or line by line from any other format (text-lines). ALTO, JSON, TXT → TXT Extracting 4 Classify every text line A CPU pre-filter labels blank lines Empty, and numbers, dates, codes and stamps Non-text, with no model. Every other line gets its language, a quality score from structural checks, character-level measures and a language model's perplexity, and one of the other three categories. The batch pipeline then revises the labels against the rest of the document. TXT → CSV Text Categorization 5 Aggregate The line categories are counted per page, with page averages, in one table for the collection and one per document, so a collection can be judged at a glance. CSV → CSV Aggregating

The five categories:

Category What it means for the line Clear legible; ready to be processed by further NLP Noisy readable, with recognition errors to correct Trash illegible; worth re-processing with another OCR Non-text not language — numbers, codes, stamps, dates Empty only whitespace; can be ignored

The service and the batch pipeline. Both run the same pre-filter and score a line with the same function. A line the pre-filter settles carries the score 0.0 and the language N/A. The document passes of step 4 are batch only: the service answers each line on its own, so over a whole document its categories can differ from a batch run's.

Perplexity in batches. The language model scores lines in batches (in the service, PPL_BATCH_LINES lines, 32 since v1.12.0-beta). A batch that runs out of memory is split in halves and retried. A line that fails even on its own gets perplexity 99999, the worst quality, and the service names it in the response's limits_applied.

Known limits. The rules were calibrated on Czech archaeological reports with German and English passages, and several of them act on every line whatever its language. A clean English, German or French line can read Noisy, and a German compound Trash; the categorisation reference lists the foreign-language cases. A Clear on a line of one to three words without Czech diacritics is less certain than the label suggests.

docs.title: Provenance and licence
docs.text:
The steps write paradata logs, and a whole-pipeline run merges them into one run summary. The service writes no paradata file: every response carries its provenance as paradata, one Process Run Crate action. The paradata lists the components the run used, each with its licence, as declared in the tool's setup/para_config.txt. The language-identification model (CC BY-NC 4.0) is used on every run. The layout-aware reading-order model (LayoutLMv3-based, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) is the batch pipeline's default method for ALTO, and the service orders ALTO uploads with it unless a request asks for ALTO's own order (reading_order=alto, since v1.13.0-beta). The GLM method uses the GLM-4 model, whose licence is also non-commercial; the other models and readers are permissive. The computed label in the paradata, the most restrictive of these licences, is not the licence of the output: Licences and paradata.

In the document record the tool originates the positional text layer of a scanned document: the pages, content, lines and tables blocks. Its blocks are stamped ocr-postprocess; records written before the rename keep alto-postprocess, which the record contract accepts as the same writer. A born-digital record is originated by digital-convert: there the tool writes only into the pages flagged needs_ocr, whose lines it replaces, and POST /score_record adds the category, score and language of the existing lines and the score and band of their pages, never their text. As the owner of the quality model it also writes quality_summary on every origin (atrium-project#73, v1.10.0-beta): page-score statistics and line counts per category, recomputed from the record whenever it writes or scores pages and lines. It is numbers only, with no band or threshold, and nothing in the pipeline routes on it.

docs.title: Where it sits
docs.text:
• Second stage of the scanned-document pipeline, and the point where the files fan out — Pipelines → W1.
  • One route of format adaptation for documents that are not ALTO — Pipelines → W11.
  • The OCR hand-off of the born-digital route. A page digital-convert flags needs_ocr is OCR'd, and its ALTO comes here with the record: the page's lines are replaced by the OCR lines, and the other pages are left as the converter wrote them — Pipelines → W3.
  • The quality model of the born-digital route. When digital-convert is set to call it, its POST /describe sends the record to POST /score_record, which scores the converter's lines with the same five categories as OCR lines — Pipelines → W2.
  • ALTO post-processing and quality control step of the AMČR text workflow 0xSpVP.

The closest tools already in Galaxy are the OCR tools that produce ALTO — tesseract, and the Kraken tools in the Digital Humanities section — which would sit directly before this workflow; no Galaxy tool classifies OCR quality line by line. The container is the service image ghcr.io/ufal/atrium-ocr-postprocess-api:<version> (POST /process, POST /score_record), where <version> is the release without its leading v; it is a CPU build. docs.title: Sorting archive pages for content-specific processing
docs.text: The page-classification workflow. Tool section: page-classification.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Archival documents mix typed reports, handwritten notes, printed forms, tables, drawings, maps and photographs, and each kind of page needs a different treatment: OCR for printed or typed text, handwritten text recognition for manuscripts, table extraction for forms, image extraction for drawings and photographs. This workflow looks at every scanned page and assigns it one of eleven categories, so that each page can be sent to the processing chain that suits it before any of that processing is run. It works on the page image alone, so the language of the page does not matter.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: In page images (PNG, JPEG, TIFF or any format Pillow reads), one file per page, named <document>-<page> or <document>_<page>; or a PDF, which the command line and the HTTP service both render page by page Out a table of the top-ranked categories and their scores per page (CSV); optionally a table of all eleven scores; a paradata log (JSON); optionally the ATRIUM document record (JSON). The HTTP service answers in JSON, with the call's provenance Runs as a command-line tool (run.py); a container image, which also runs a Galaxy job script; an HTTP service image; an Agent Skill Compute CPU is enough; a GPU makes large batches faster Network fetches the fine-tuned models from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, then works from its cache; or reads models staged once in a folder, offline (--models-dir) Code licence MIT Component licences the code and the fine-tuned models are MIT; the LINDAT training dataset (CC BY-NC 4.0) is used only for training; the optional YOLO backend is AGPL-3.0; the service renders PDFs with pypdfium2 (Apache-2.0). These do not by themselves set the rights in the output: Licences and paradata Record SSH Open Marketplace tool RER7Fw

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
# Step What happens In → out Activity 1 Prepare the page images A PDF is rendered to one image per page with pypdfium2 at 300 dpi (PDF_RENDER_DPI), by the command line (-f report.pdf, or -ff pdf for a folder) and the HTTP service alike; --pages (pages) selects part of it. The bundled converters (data_scripts/: pdftoppm on Unix, ImageMagick with Ghostscript on Windows) remain for preparing training pages. Each image is named after its document and page number, <document>-<page>.png; the number after the last - or _ becomes the page number in every result. PDF → PNG, JPEG Converting 2 Choose the model One fine-tuned model — a named revision of ufal/vit-historical-page — or the five-model ensemble (--best, or version=all, the service's default), which averages the scores of revisions v1.4–v5.4: three Vision Transformers, a RegNetY and an EfficientNetV2. Naming a revision explicitly keeps results reproducible. — — 3 Classify the pages Each image is resized to the model's input size, scored for all eleven categories, and the scores are turned into probabilities. The highest-ranked categories (three by default) are kept with their scores, best first. A single page, a folder or a whole tree can be processed. PNG, JPEG → CSV Identifying 4 Review the results The result table gives each page's best category (CLASS-1) and its confidence (SCORE-1). A low top score with a close second marks a page worth a human look; the all-scores table and, with the ensemble, one vote per model make disagreement visible. CSV → CSV — 5 Route the pages Each category calls for its own processing chain (table below). The classifier does not move pages itself: the decision is taken by a person or a script reading the result table. CSV → — — 6 Record provenance Every command-line run writes a paradata log with the tool version, run id, configuration, statistics, skipped files and the resolved licence; the HTTP service writes no file and returns the same record in its answer. On request the run also writes its block of the ATRIUM document record, which later pipeline stages build on. → JSON —

What each category suggests doing next:

Category Typical next step TEXT_P, TEXT_T OCR for printed or typewritten text TEXT_HW handwritten text recognition (HTR) TEXT both — the page mixes printed, typed and handwritten text LINE_P, LINE_T table or form extraction, with OCR for the cells LINE_HW table or form extraction, with HTR for the cells DRAW, PHOTO image extraction; captions, if any, through OCR DRAW_L, PHOTO_L image extraction plus table extraction for the surrounding layout or legend

The labels themselves, and how the models were trained, are on the tool's Overview.

Two side workflows use the same tool: training and evaluating a model on one's own labelled pages (Pipelines → W8), and turning PDFs into a labelled training set and corrections back into it (Pipelines → W12).

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• A routing decision per page — the Top-N table (FILE, PAGE, CLASS-1…N, SCORE-1…N), one row per page, best guess first. The HTTP service gives the same per page in JSON.
  • Evidence for review — the all-scores table, and, with the command-line ensemble, each model's own vote.
  • A provenance record — the paradata log of the run, or the paradata of a service answer, with each component's licence.
  • A document record (on request) — page_categories maps each page to its label, and every page carries its category and confidence, ready for the next stage to build on.

Every column is described in Reference → Outputs.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• One category per page. A page that combines, say, a photograph and running text gets the category of what dominates; the categories with the _L suffix and TEXT exist for the common mixtures.
  • Neighbouring categories are the hard cases. Most errors fall between categories that look alike, TEXT and TEXT_T above all.
  • The categories come from one kind of archive. They were formed from archival documents of 1920–2020; pages of a very different kind are forced into the nearest category.
  • PDFs are rendered with a different engine. The training pages were made with pdftoppm; the service and, since v1.10.3-beta, the command line use pypdfium2, which is about as close to pdftoppm in pixels as PyMuPDF, the engine it replaced. On 2,514 pages of 15 born-digital AMČR reports, pypdfium2 and PyMuPDF gave the same top-1 label on 2,509 pages; the other five moved to a neighbouring category. The tool's data_scripts/pdf_rasteriser_comparison.md holds the measurements.
  • A PDF request classifies at most 50 pages. That is the default of MAX_PDF_PAGES; a longer PDF is refused (413) before any page is rendered, and the pages field classifies part of it instead. An upload is at most 10 MB by default (MAX_UPLOAD_MB). The command line has no such cap.
  • Truncated images. The command-line tool classifies a truncated scan, its missing part filled grey; the HTTP service refuses it (422).
  • The ensemble can answer with fewer models. If one of the five models fails, the others are averaged: in the service, and since v1.12.0-beta in the command line's --best too, which stopped before. Since v1.9.10-beta the answer's models_used lists the revisions that answered (per page for a PDF); the service log names the failing model, once, and the command line the models that answered. Before v1.9.4-beta, on a GPU node, every model fetched from the Hub failed this way.

docs.title: Translating XML documents with a protected domain vocabulary
docs.text: The translator workflow. Tool section: translator.

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Archival collections hold text inside XML: OCR transcriptions in ALTO XML, and structured metadata records such as those of the Archaeological Map of the Czech Republic (AMČR). This workflow translates that text — into English by default — and writes it back into the same document, so that tags, namespaces, attributes and, for ALTO, the position of every word survive, and the result stays valid against its schema. Domain terms can be held to their established translations from a controlled vocabulary, so that an archaeological term is rendered the same way in every document.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: In ALTO XML pages, or any well-formed XML with a list of the fields to translate (XPaths), told apart by their root element unless a mode is named; files, folders or lists of URLs; optionally a vocabulary (CSV) Out the translated document (same format); a translation log pairing source and target text (CSV); a paradata log (JSON); the ATRIUM document record (JSON). The service returns the log and the record on request (include_log, include_record) Runs as a command-line tool (main.py); a container image; an HTTP service image (POST /translate); an Agent Skill Compute CPU; a GPU only for a self-hosted translation model (Qwen3.8-27B was measured on one 96 GB GPU) Network the LINDAT translation service (the default backend) and the LINDAT UDPipe service (vocabulary matching), or the server of a language-model backend; the Hugging Face Hub for the language-identification model on first use, from a checkout (the published images carry it); GitHub when the vocabulary is fetched from keyword-extract's release Code licence MIT Component licences a default run uses CUBBITT through the LINDAT service (a CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 model, under LINDAT's terms of use) and, when the source language is detected, FastText (CC BY-NC 4.0); a run with only permissive components can be assembled (see below). These do not by themselves set the rights in the output: Licences and paradata Records SSH Open Marketplace tool CizIUW and workflow 13eHAZ

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
# Step What happens In → out Activity 1 Prepare a domain vocabulary (optional) Czech–English term pairs from the AMČR vocabularies and the TEATER thesaurus, each pointing back to the concept it came from. The project keeps one curated list, which keyword-extract publishes with each release: load_vocab.py --from-release builds the CSV from that asset, checked against its .sha256, and adds the concept's description where there is one. The bundled harvester collects pairs from the live sources instead (AMČR over OAI-PMH, TEATER over GraphQL). The shipped data_samples/vocabulary.csv is keyword-extract's v1.3.0-beta list: 4,715 pairs, 1,961 with a description. A vocabulary of one's own in the same CSV form works as well. → CSV Collecting 2 Choose the mode and the fields ALTO transcriptions are translated in ALTO mode, which works on the words of each text line. For metadata records, the fields to translate are listed as XPaths; namespaces and OAI-PMH envelopes are handled by the tool. The file's root element decides the mode (an <alto> root is ALTO, any other is metadata) unless one is named: --alto, --xpaths or --formats on the command line, is_alto in the service (since v1.6.0-beta). ALTO, XML — 3 Identify the source language A language-identification model detects the language of each text block (ALTO) or field (metadata), so a record that mixes languages is handled piece by piece. A guess is used only when it is confident and names a language the backend translates; otherwise the element's own label, the document's language, then a configured default decide. A confident guess of a language the backend cannot translate is reported for review. Naming the source language skips detection. Before anything is translated, the named language, or the default, is checked against the backend: a pair it cannot translate is refused (exit 1 on the command line, 422 unsupported_language_pair from the service) and is never rerouted. — — 4 Protect domain terms (optional) Vocabulary terms found in the text are replaced by placeholders before translation and restored as their agreed translations afterwards; multi-word terms are matched first, single words by lemma. Language-model backends receive the matching terms as a glossary in the prompt instead; the OpenAI-compatible backend can add each term's description as context (off by default). The command line takes the vocabulary with --vocabulary; the service applies one only when VOCABULARY_PATH names it. CSV Lemmatizing 5 Translate The text goes to the chosen backend: the LINDAT translation service (CUBBITT, the default), an OpenAI-compatible language-model API (such as Qwen3.8-27B on one's own vLLM server), or a self-hosted CTranslate2 model. Long texts are split at sentence boundaries first. Every reply is checked against its source: one that is empty, runaway, cut short, looping, or mixes Latin and Cyrillic letters in a word is requested again, re-run at the end of the document if it still fails, and never written. — Translating 6 Rebuild and validate the document ALTO: each text block is translated as a whole and line by line; the fluent whole-block translation is then divided among the original lines and written into the original word elements — replacing their text, or added beside it as an alternative. Metadata: the translation replaces the source text, or is added beside it with language labels. Metadata output can be validated against an XSD schema, such as the AMČR schema, which accepts replaced records and not appended ones: --xsd on the command line, XSD_PATH in the service (since v1.6.0-beta). → ALTO, XML — 7 Review and record provenance A translation log beside each output pairs source and target text line by line or field by field, with a status saying whether each was translated normally, recovered by a re-run, placed approximately, kept as source, or translated from a fallback language because the backend cannot translate the detected one. The paradata log records what was run, with each component's licence; the document record notes the languages, the backend, the translated file and the same component licences. → CSV, JSON —

Which backend. LINDAT stays the default. The recommended self-hosted alternative is openai_compatible with Qwen3.8-27B (Apache-2.0) on one's own vLLM server: in the bake-off of 2026-10-19 it kept numbers and vocabulary terms about as well as LINDAT (terms 0.978 against 0.987) and failed no segment. ct2 with EuroLLM is no longer recommended, because it drops short segments (see Limits). The bake-off compares the backends without reference translations. Its script is eval/bakeoff.py, its results are in eval/results/issue4_bakeoff_2610/, and the decision is in the tool's docs/translation-backends.md.

The vocabulary step is its own workflow on Pipelines — W7, vocabulary harvesting and review.

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• The same document in another language — <name>_<target language>.<extension>, every tag and namespace in place; for ALTO, every line where it was.
  • A review log — <name>_log.csv, with the source and the translated text side by side, and a status per line that points a reviewer at what was recovered, approximated, left untranslated or translated from a fallback language.
  • Consistent terminology — every protected term carries its agreed translation, and the paradata counts the protected terms per document.
  • A provenance record — the paradata log of the run, with each component's licence, and a document record per file, <name>.document.json.

The translator's output is an end product: an edition for readers and for publication. No later stage of the pipeline reads it; the document record refers to it.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Word positions in translated ALTO are approximate. Line boundaries are exact; how the words of a line are spread over its word elements is constructed, because a translation has a different number of words.
  • Schema validation applies to metadata output. ALTO output keeps the structure of its input — and is valid ALTO in either mode — but is not validated by the tool. The command line takes a schema file or URL (--xsd); the service, since v1.6.0-beta, only a local file its deployment names (XSD_PATH), and answers xsd_valid (or refuses with xsd_strict).
  • Appended AMČR records are not valid AMČR. The AMČR schema allows neither a language label on the translated fields nor a second copy of them; a record that must validate is translated in replace mode.
  • Language coverage is the backend's. Into English, LINDAT translates from Czech, German, French, Polish, Russian and Ukrainian. A pair the backend has no model for is refused, not routed through Czech; other pairs need another backend.
  • Placeholders protect terms only for the LINDAT backend. Language-model backends get a glossary instead, and the self-hosted neural translation models receive no vocabulary.
  • EuroLLM on ct2 drops short segments. In the bake-off EuroLLM-9B ran on past the source in 96 of 1,230 segments, almost all a number or a single word. The guard keeps their source text and logs them untranslated.

A run with only permissive components needs both: a self-hosted model under a permissive licence and the source language named explicitly. The recommended model is Qwen3.8-27B through openai_compatible, recorded with LLM_LICENSE_COMPONENT=qwen3_8; a ct2 model of the EuroLLM, MADLAD-400 or Opus-MT family also qualifies. The AMČR and TEATER vocabularies are CC0 and do not stand in its way. How the label is computed is on Reference → Licence.

In the document record the tool owns the translations block and records the translated file as derived_from.translated_xml. The block also counts the segments in a language the backend cannot translate (unsupported_source_langs).
